notes: The towns’ names participate in a dense series of soundplays: dust, beauty and shame, going out, bitterness, horses, deception, and possession. The names are retained rather than replaced by invented English towns. Several short clauses, especially concerning Beth-ezel, remain difficult.

Verse 10 follows the traditional read imperative “roll yourself,” rather than the written first-person form. The bird in verse 16 is rendered vulture because of the baldness image; the Hebrew bird term also commonly denotes an eagle.
vocabulary: Prostitute’s wages
The poem depicts wealth associated with false worship through a sexual-economic image.
Daughter Zion
Jerusalem and its people portrayed as a woman.

notes: The land recipient called a renegade is uncertain. Speaker divisions in verses 6–7 are not marked in Hebrew. Verse 8’s garment and war-return wording is difficult; the draft preserves a reading without disguising its uncertainty.
The sheep enclosure can also be read as the place-name Bozrah. The breakthrough, king, and LORD at the head are retained without assigning the unnamed figures identities beyond the passage.
vocabulary: Measuring line and lot
Means of dividing and assigning land within the community.
Pour out words
The Hebrew uses a verb of dripping for prophetic speech, here turned against unwanted preaching.

notes: The butchery and eating of human flesh form an extended image of rulers consuming their people. The graphic details are retained rather than replaced with an abstract reference to exploitation.
The prophets’ peace depends on food in their mouths; those who do not feed them receive a declaration of war. Covering the upper lip is a gesture of grief or shame.
vocabulary: Justice
Right judgment and treatment of others, the responsibility repeatedly charged to the leaders.
Temple mountain
The mountain associated with the sanctuary; the next chapter reverses the image of its desolation.

notes: The passage shares much language with Isaiah 2. Its own details are preserved, including distant powerful nations, the vine and fig tree, and the declaration about walking in God’s name.
The tower and stronghold are not precisely identified. Verse 13’s final verb is first person in the pinned text: “I will devote,” although other readings take the subject as Zion.
vocabulary: Plowshares; pruning hooks
Tools for cultivation, made here from weapons; Joel 3:10 reverses this image in a call to battle.
Redeem
Rescue from another’s power, here explicitly promised at Babylon.

notes: Verse 1 is 4:14 in the Hebrew source. Its opening can refer to mustering troops or cutting oneself in mourning. Bethlehem’s ruler has origins “from ancient days”; the phrase does not by itself settle all later understandings of the ruler’s identity or duration of existence. The woman in labor is unnamed.
Seven and eight form an escalating number pair. Verse 6 follows “entrances,” not a different reading involving drawn swords. Verse 14 retains “cities” rather than emending to idols.
vocabulary: Shepherd
An image for governing and protecting the people.
Asherah poles
Cult objects associated with Asherah, here marked for removal.

notes: The questions escalate from offerings to the speaker’s firstborn. The response names justice, faithful kindness, and humble walking; the question about a child is not a command to offer one.

These lines contain difficult wording. Verse 9 retains seeing the name, rod, and its appointer; alternatives involve fearing the name or addressing a tribe. Verse 11 keeps the first-person “be pure.” The inward emptiness and saving clauses in verse 14 also admit different readings.
vocabulary: Shittim to Gilgal
Places bracketing Israel’s entry into the land in the remembered journey.
Ephah and weights
Tools of trade whose manipulation makes the charge of dishonesty concrete.

notes: The enemy is grammatically feminine, like a personified city. The boundary/decree term in verse 11 and Egypt/fortified-city wording in verse 12 are uncertain. The draft preserves the geographical promise without adding a modern map.
The source shifts between “you” and “him,” then between “our” guilt and “their” sins. These shifts are retained rather than silently harmonized.
vocabulary: Inheritance
The people are pictured as the flock belonging to God.
Who is a God like you?
The question echoes the meaning of Micah’s name and introduces the final praise of forgiveness.

sections.18: Who is a God like you?
